questions.topic: Stating hypotheses, Type I/II errors and level of significance
questions.text: What are the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis?
questions.ideal_answer: The null hypothesis, H0, is the default statement that there is no effect, no difference or no relationship, for example that the mean equals 50. The alternative hypothesis, H1 or Ha, is the claim we want to find evidence for, that there is an effect or difference, for example that the mean is not 50. A hypothesis test uses sample data to decide whether to reject H0 in favour of H1. We never prove H0; we either reject it or fail to reject it.

questions.topic: P-values, rejection regions and critical values
questions.ideal_answer: A p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. A small p-value means the observed data would be unlikely if H0 were true, which is evidence against H0. If the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level alpha, such as 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis. The p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.

questions.topic: Stating hypotheses, Type I/II errors and level of significance
questions.text: What is the difference between a Type I error and a Type II error?
questions.ideal_answer: A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true, a false positive, and its probability is the significance level alpha. A Type II error is failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false, a false negative, and its probability is beta. For example, convicting an innocent person is like a Type I error and acquitting a guilty person is like a Type II error. The power of a test is 1 minus beta, and for a fixed sample size reducing alpha increases beta.

questions.topic: z-test and t-test for a mean
questions.text: When do you use a z-test and when do you use a t-test for a mean?
questions.ideal_answer: A z-test is used when the population standard deviation is known, or when the sample size is large, usually above 30, so the sample standard deviation is a good estimate. A t-test is used when the population standard deviation is unknown and estimated from the sample, especially for small samples. The t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution and depends on degrees of freedom, n minus 1 for a one-sample test. As the sample size grows, the t-distribution approaches the normal distribution.

questions.topic: Contingency tables: chi-square, Fisher's exact and McNemar's tests
questions.text: How does a chi-square test of independence work on a contingency table?
questions.ideal_answer: The null hypothesis is that the two categorical variables are independent. For each cell, the expected frequency is calculated as row total times column total divided by the grand total. The test statistic is the sum over all cells of (observed minus expected) squared divided by expected. It is compared with the chi-square distribution with (rows minus 1) times (columns minus 1) degrees of freedom, and a large value or small p-value leads to rejecting independence; if expected counts are below 5, Fisher's exact test is preferred.

questions.text: How would you perform a two-sample t-test in Python and interpret the result?
questions.ideal_answer: In Python we can use scipy.stats.ttest_ind, passing the two samples, which returns the t statistic and the p-value. If variances are not assumed equal, we set equal_var=False to run Welch's t-test. If the p-value is below the chosen significance level, such as 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis that the two population means are equal. We should also check assumptions such as approximate normality and independence of the samples.

questions.topic: Non-parametric tests: Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney U and sign test
questions.text: Why would you choose the Mann-Whitney U test instead of an independent two-sample t-test?
questions.ideal_answer: The t-test assumes the data in each group are approximately normally distributed and is sensitive to outliers. The Mann-Whitney U test is a non-parametric test that uses the ranks of the combined data instead of raw values, so it does not require normality. It is preferred for small samples from skewed distributions, data with outliers, or ordinal data such as ratings. It tests whether one group tends to have larger values than the other, often interpreted as a difference in medians, but it has somewhat less power than the t-test when data really are normal.

questions.text: Why do we use ANOVA instead of running multiple t-tests to compare the means of three or more groups?
questions.ideal_answer: Running many pairwise t-tests inflates the overall Type I error rate, because each test has a chance of a false positive, and with three groups at alpha 0.05 the family-wise error rate is about 14%. One-way ANOVA tests all group means in a single test with the null hypothesis that all means are equal. It compares between-group variance with within-group variance using the F statistic. If ANOVA is significant, post-hoc tests like Tukey's HSD identify which groups differ while controlling the error rate.

questions.topic: Goodness-of-fit tests: chi-square, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Shapiro-Wilk, Anderson-Darling
questions.text: You have 10,000 observations and the Shapiro-Wilk test rejects normality with a very small p-value, though the histogram looks almost normal. How should you interpret this?
questions.ideal_answer: With very large samples, normality tests like Shapiro-Wilk have very high power, so even tiny, practically unimportant departures from normality become statistically significant. Statistical significance is not the same as practical importance. I would check normality visually using a histogram and Q-Q plot, and look at skewness and kurtosis values. Also, with large samples the central limit theorem makes tests on means robust to mild non-normality, so a t-test or ANOVA can usually still be used.

questions.topic: Non-parametric ANOVA: Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman, Mood's median
questions.text: Three groups have skewed data with unequal variances and outliers. Which test would you use to compare them, and what if the same subjects were measured under all three conditions?
questions.ideal_answer: Since ANOVA assumptions of normality and equal variances are violated, I would use the Kruskal-Wallis test, the non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA that compares groups using ranks. Mood's median test is another option that is even more robust to outliers but has less power. If the same subjects were measured under all three conditions, the data are repeated measures, so the Friedman test should be used instead. If the test is significant, post-hoc pairwise tests such as Dunn's test with a correction like Bonferroni are used.

questions.topic: Regression and smoothing: ridge, GLM, Poisson regression, GAM
questions.text: An app company wants to model the number of daily crashes per device based on OS version and memory. Which regression model would you use and why?
questions.ideal_answer: The response is a count of non-negative integers, so ordinary linear regression is not ideal because it can predict negative values and assumes constant variance and normal errors. A Poisson regression, a generalized linear model with a log link, is suitable for count data. If the variance is much larger than the mean, known as overdispersion, a negative binomial or quasi-Poisson model should be used. Coefficients are interpreted as multiplicative effects on the expected crash rate, and an offset can account for different usage time per device.

questions.topic: Communicating results: data storytelling and infographics
questions.text: An A/B test shows a statistically significant 0.2% increase in conversion. How would you present this to non-technical managers and what would you caution them about?
questions.ideal_answer: I would start with the business question and the result in plain language, such as the new design increased conversion from 5.0% to 5.2%, and show it with a simple chart and a confidence interval rather than just a p-value. I would explain that statistical significance means the effect is unlikely to be due to chance, but it does not guarantee the effect is practically important. I would estimate the business impact, like additional revenue, against the cost of the change. I would also caution about effect size, test duration, novelty effects, and the risk of false positives from checking results repeatedly.
